f896d0f44a21babfa0104e0571dcde17.text: You may hear or see a CC-295 Kingfisher airplane southwest of Williams Lake dropping smoke or illumination flares as the Canadian Armed Forces train in the Chilcotin Range from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20. Airplanes may be seen dropping smoke or illumination flares west of Williams Lake in the coming days as the Canadian Armed Forces train in the sky. According to a public service announcement, aircraft from 19 Wing Comox will be training from Monday, Nov. 16 to Friday, Nov. 20 between 6 p.m. and 1 a.m. in the Chilcotin Military Training Area to maintain their night operation capabilities. “During this period, members of the public may hear or see one of the squadron’s CC-295 Kingfisher airplanes in the area dropping smoke or illumination flares,” the announcement stated. “These bright white flares can be seen from a great distance as they slowly descend from the sky to the water and burn for four to five minutes each.” The essential training will ensure the Royal Canadian Air Force’s (RCAF) Search and Rescue (SAR) crews are able to safely conduct night rescues. “RCAF SAR Technicians are known for their distinctive bright orange jumpsuits and commitment to helping Canadians in peril,” the announcement further added. “Regular training under a variety of conditions ensures that the SAR techs are always ready to meet whatever challenges, day or night, that a mission may present.”

29329d980313831e5ab4a0e75c0066c5.text: A “communication issue” has led to a ground stop for all U.S. airport by the Federal Aviation Administration. The grounding of flights at all U.S. airports is beginning to have international impacts. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop Friday afternoon (Nov. 13), citing telecommunications issues. The agency said in a post to X that a temporary telecommunications outage has led to the ground stop “out of an abundance of caution.” The post adds that every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis. The post did not say when the outage could be resolved or when the ground stop could be lifted. An update had not been provided by 5:36 p.m. Pacific Time. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy posted to social media at 2:16 p.m. Pacific Time that the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following the “communication issue” that is impacting all air route traffic control centres. He added that Federal Aviation Administration technicians are investigating the issue. U.S.-bound flights are showing as “delayed” on multiple major Canadian airport departure flight trackers. Vancouver International Airport says it’s seeing delays for U.S.-bound flights, as well as some international routes that would fly over U.S. airspace. Initially, the airport said domestic flights are not impacted. However, an update at 5:11 p.m. from YVR says “airlines are adjusting flight schedules accordingly, which is causing cancellations to U.S. destinations, and some delays and cancellations to international and domestic flights at YVR. Toronto Pearson International Airport says international and domestic flights are continuing to operate out of the airport “where routes do not require transit through U.S. airspace.”

c694d23a6de94123bbe1ec3cac6ad0c0.text: Members of the Okanagan Indian Band filled a small courtroom in Kelowna the morning of Nov. 13 to listen to the appeal for a man no longer allowed in their community. Donald Ashley, a First Nations healer, appeared at the Kelowna Law Courts to appeal his 2025 sentence for simple assault of a client in 2022. Ashley was originally charged with six counts of sexual assault for allegations of inappropriate touching of six complainants during one-on-one healing sessions in October 2022. One of the charges was stayed at the start of the trial, and two more charges were dropped according to the direction of the presiding judge. Ashley was found guilty by a jury in 2024 of one count of simple assault. Sentenced later that year, as reported by IndigiNews, Ashley did not receive any jail time, but a two-year probation order with a one-year ban on offering healing sessions and the second-year order requiring healing sessions to be conducted with supervision and client-signed waivers. Defence counsel for Ashley, Mark Iyengar and Mark Nohra, argued the sentence issued was an error in judgement by the sentencing judge and demonstrably unfit for the charge, requesting a discharge. Iyengar told the three-judge panel that his client’s sentence was issued in error and more weight should have been placed on the therapeutic context of the touching. Defence stated the inference should be made that the touching was for healing purposes and not for self-gratification. Defence also argued the community impact statement was incorrectly considered by the sentencing judge, as it had been edited before being submitted to the court and the overall sentiment had changed. Nohra followed his colleague by stating that Ashley’s sentence was demonstrably unfit, having caused him mental health struggles, financial hardships, and a disconnect from his Indigenous roots as he’s been banned from all Okanagan band territories. Sturko ran as CentreBC leader in the Surrey South riding in the Oct. 24 provincial election, a seat won by former White Rock mayor and Conservative candidate Megan Knight. “I’m leaving partisan politics. d87e0c7babbcf15c9616d76b23e54bdd.text: Nelson track runner Matti Erickson has signed a pro contract with Nike. Now that his college career is over, Matti Erickson’s race is only just starting. The Nelson, B.C., track star has signed a pro contract with Nike Swoosh TC, which is the sportswear giant’s distance running team. The deal will see Erickson compete for Nike through 2028. Erickson graduated from the University of Oregon this year and considered becoming a math teacher, but ultimately decided that, at 23 years old, he still has plenty of track ahead of him. “I thought I’m just too far along in this journey to give up now,” he said. “I have unfinished business, unaccomplished goals that I still feel like I have the ability to accomplish even if they feel far away. And so for those reasons, I just feel like I’ve got too much in me still. I’m so unproven that it was no-brainer really.” Erickson was a star for the Oregon Ducks, during which he was also the first Canadian athlete to sign a name, image and likeness deal with Nike. He won the 800-metres race at the 2025 NCAA indoor championships, and that year also won silver in the outdoor championships. Erickson also competed for Canada at the World Athletics Championships in 2025. But his last season was hampered by injuries, which forced Erickson to pull out of the world indoor championships in Poland in March, and for Team Canada at the summer’s Commonwealth Games in Scotland. Erickson said he is healthy again, and will have plenty of time to prepare for his next race. “I’ve got a big chunk of time to just really dial in on the training, get used to the new program and new dynamics with the training partners and really focus on being as healthy as possible and maintaining the level of health that I do have right now.” Qualifying for and excelling at the World Athletics Championships, which is next held September 2027 in Beijing, is among Erickson’s goals for the coming year. Erickson failed to make it to the semifinals at the 2025 worlds in Tokyo.

e133fa6eb10c0e0e8c6b82820e989916.text: The northwest corner of the Pear Lake wildfire, pictured on July 31. A preliminary report into the post-wildfire hazards associated with the fire has now been released, indicating likely moderate to high impacts on local properties, highways, and infrastructure. A preliminary assessment of the post-wildfire hazards of the Pear Lake wildfire near Clinton this past summer show that homes, highways, and infrastructure such as the CN rail line and a BC Hydro substation are at elevated risk from flooding, debris flows, and landslides in the fire’s aftermath. The Pear Lake wildfire was reported on July 17, and was not declared under control until Sept. 14. It burned a total area of 165,909 hectares (1,659 square kilometres), forced the evacuation of thousands of residents, and destroyed more than 120 structures, including homes. The report — dated Oct. 8 and released on Nov. 9 — is largely based on aerial reconnaissance carried out in August. The report’s author, geomorphologist Sarah Crookshanks, notes that it was prepared on an expedited basis so that a Level 4 Detailed Assessment can be started. The fire affected 28 watersheds, with some seeing up to 99 per cent of their area burned. The Clinton Creek watershed (6,663 hectares) saw 86 per cent of its area burned, with 76 per cent of that burned at moderate or high severity. Some 50 per cent of the Big Bar Creek watershed (45,156 hectares in total) was burned, and 41 per cent of the Maiden Creek watershed (5,955 hectares) was burned. The report states that potential elements at risk include residential structures on private properties; First Nations lands; the Highway 97 and Highway 99 corridors; secondary public roads, including the Clinton-Pavilion Road and the southern part of Jesmond Road; provincial parks at Marble Range, Big Bar Lake, Downing, and Chasm; the CN rail mainline; the BC Hydro transmission line and substation near Kelly Lake; and water resources and infrastructure in the Clinton Community Watershed.

Police in Vancouver, along with the help of international partners, cracked down on a Russia-based cybercrime network. The RCMP Federal Policing Pacific Region cybercrime investigation team in Vancouver is the lead Canadian police agency in the international joint forces operation targeting initial access malware. It was dubbed Operation Endgame, according to a news release from RCMP Friday (Nov. 13). The Vancouver team contributed coders, analysts and investigators. Police say the Russia-based “Gootloader” malware enables unauthorized access to computer systems around the world through compromised websites. It uses infected WordPress websites to spread malware “masquerading as legal documents.” The team in Vancouver and the RCMP’s cyber and technical investigation service developed a tool that removes Gootloader malware from infected machines. That tool was then shared with Operation Endgame partners to “disrupt the malware on a global scale.” The week of Nov. 9, the police team from Vancouver were at Europol headquarters in The Hague, Netherlands to participate in global action week when the “disinfection tool” was deployed by law enforcement in Canada, Denmark, The Netherlands and the U.S. Police said during that time, approximately 672 infected websites were remediated globally. In Canada, the Vancouver team disinfected 24 compromised machines. RCMP added that Operation Endgame is the largest ongoing joint forces operation that has brought together law enforcement agencies from countries including Canada, Bulgaria, Denmark, Germany, Netherlands, Poland, the United Kingdom and the U.S. It’s supported by Europol and Eurojust. The Vancouver team has previously helped with Operation Endgame earlier this year, working to crack down on SocGholish, which is linked to the Russian cybercriminal group Evil Corp. Victoria has been recognized as one of North America’s top 10 fairytale cities, thanks to its British-inspired architecture, historic landmarks and waterfront scenery. Travel Off Path released its list of 10 Fairytale Cities in North America on Oct. 31, placing Victoria seventh among destinations in Canada, the United States and Mexico. The B.C. Parliament Buildings overlooking the Inner Harbour were also highlighted for giving the city a regal, old-world atmosphere. Fox suggested visitors explore Victoria’s waterfront dining options rather than spend money on some of the city’s more expensive tourist experiences. Instead, he recommended visiting a local waterfront pub for fish and chips and a locally brewed beer. Victoria was one of three Canadian destinations included in the ranking. 3ca52d080a8bd836a67977ae457ade64.text: A West Kelowna woman was fined $368 when she was spotted driving with an open laptop on her lap during a traffic stop in Vernon on Nov. 5. Many people are still working remotely, but BC Highway Patrol (BCHP) is reminding drivers that vehicles are not offices, and using your laptop while operating a vehicle could land you with a steep fine. A 52-year-old West Kelowna woman found that out the hard way, and is now facing a $368 fine for allegedly driving while using her laptop during a recent BCHP distracted driving operation in Vernon. The stop occurred on Nov. 5, just after 4:30 p.m., when a BC Highway Patrol officer observed a blue Honda Pilot whose driver had an open laptop on her lap on Highway 97 (32 Street) in Vernon. “Driving is a complex task that requires your complete attention to deal with the unexpected,” says Sgt. Michael McLaughlin with BC Highway Patrol. “Just because you’re comfortable behind the wheel, and you have something you ‘need’ to do, doesn’t mean the rules of the road don’t apply to you.” The driver of the blue Honda was issued a ticket for use of an electronic device while driving, which comes with a fine of $368. The ticket also includes four penalty points on their driver’s licence. Drivers who have two or more distracted driving tickets in a three-year period will also pay a Driver Risk Premium. This could see the total financial penalty rise to as much as $2,000, in addition to the regular insurance premium. While much of the focus of distracted driving campaigns is on the use of cell phones, BCHP wants to remind drivers that “electronic devices” include a lot of different things. “Prescribed electronic devices in the BC Motor Vehicle Act include televisions, electronic logging devices, and any hand-held device that can process or compute data,” says McLaughlin. “It’s astonishing that we need to remind drivers that watching TV and using your laptop is illegal, or that holding a cell phone like a piece of pizza is not ‘hands free,’ but

1bc21cf118f5daaa77c0715a4f462820.text: Spanish Mountain Gold Ltd. has redesigned its proposed open-pit gold mine near Likely that is planned to utilize filtered stack tailings technology (dry stacking). As B.C’s forestry sector continues to struggle, now is the time for mining according to the Mayor of Williams Lake as a mining exploration company seeks to develop a newly redesigned open-pit gold mine that would annually inject an estimated $190-million into the Cariboo regional economy. Spanish Mountain Gold Ltd. (SMG) has recently resumed early community engagement on its proposed open-pit gold mine near Likely northeast of Williams Lake. ”It’s mining time. You can’t go wrong,” Surinderpal Rathor said at a community open house earlier this month in Williams Lake where he was joined by Coun. Scott Nelson. SMG Vice President, Environment, Social and Governance Travis Desormeaux said SMG hopes to have a final investment decision in 2028 with construction commencing shortly after where they would likely be hiring between 750 to 1,000 jobs over a 24-month period. The mine’s utilization of filtered stack tailings technology, also known as dry stacking, is anticipated to provide up to 250 full time jobs during its planned 25-year mine life. A 2021 design previously directly impacted Boswell and Nina Lakes, which are fish-bearing, with the tailings storage facility located directly above Cedar Creek, a catchment that flows into Quesnel Lake and at its confluence sits Cedar Point Provincial Park. The Quesnel Lake Watershed was heavily impacted by a catastrophic August 2014 Mount Polley Mine tailings pond collapse which resulted in the release of millions of cubic metres of waste, and through the early engagement process in 2021 by SGM, concerns of any potential failure risks were identified. Treated mine water would also have been discharged directly into Cedar Creek, passing through the provincial park before entering Quesnel Lake. 0de8f2d202147ab871e4614232b10ce9.text: A total of 20 volunteers took to the River Valley on Friday, Nov 13 for a garbage clean up. I organized a garbage pick-up in the River Valley that attracted 20 volunteers. The city provided garbage bags, gloves, garbage pickers and a container for disposing needles. The people who showed up were eager to help and our own hometown hero Wilber Saunders was delighted to see so many people willing to lend a hand do something he does all the time. The city crew met us at 1 p.m. down on the road so we could show them that there were so many areas yet to be tackled. They were also picking up our piles on the side of the road. It is difficult to know if these areas are years old or newer. Some people dump stuff over the banks. We found flooring, fridge parts, and more. This effort came about because while doing a patrol with Community Policing my partner and I saw some areas and I muttered that it would be great to get in there before it snows. Then earlier this week, Wilber posted about picking up garbage in the River Valley and I thought, let’s do this! Thanks so much to everyone who came out. As many people remarked, it is amazing what a group of people can do in two hours. Some people gave an hour, some five. Every minute made a difference.

44601377287dfb415ca0f150bc897964.text: A man has been hospitalized after he was shot by RCMP near Kaslo on Friday. The Investigations Office of British Columbia (IIO) said in a statement Saturday that police responded to a disturbance at a residence outside Kaslo. The unidentified man allegedly exited the home with what the IIO describes as an “edged weapon.” “Officers verbally engaged with the man and during the interaction an officer discharged their service pistol.” The IIO investigates police conduct whenever a person is injured in interactions with officers.

97e7163bc97de5da532a1134332e0d25.text: Thousands of flights cancelled, delayed following grounding of all U.S. planes | Williams Lake Tribune Thousands of flights cancelled, delayed following grounding of all U.S. planes Travellers left waiting following ground stop of all U.S. flights on Nov. 13. This weekend could mean misery for thousands of travellers in the United States as some flights across the country are delayed following yesterday’s (Nov. 13) nationwide grounding of all planes, including 3,600 cancellations. ​Delta Airlines has cancelled 20 per cent of its flights for Nov. 14, while United Airlines has cancelled 17 per cent and American Airlines has cancelled 15 per cent. ​The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) called for a full ground stop due to telecommunications outages, creating a serious backlog Saturday morning; however, some domestic flights have resumed. ​A post by the FAA adds that it has accounted for every flight and will handle international flights on a case-by-case basis. ​Secretary Sean Duffy provided an update on the FAA National Ground Stop last night, and is expected to be updating the public again on Saturday at 7:30 a.m. Pacific. ​“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system. I think every single one of your networks has covered the president and myself talking about this for the last two years. The president, for the last year, has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system,” said Duffy. ​“We have TDM telecom, so this is analog telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data; they started giving us inconsistency in the data … and because of that we shut the system down.” ​The ground stop did not come from a threat to the United States and was not linked to this week’s Microsoft outage, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullen. ​Travel impacts could last several days while airports and airlines comb through thousands of cancellations and delays.

I Competed at the ‘Super Age Games’ to Find Out. Is Longevity a Sport Now? I Competed at the ‘Super Age Games’ to Find Out. Right before turning 60, I participated in events testing balance, agility and more. My score promised to tell me how well I’m aging. Is Longevity a Sport Now? I Competed at the ‘Super Age Games’ to Find Out. Right before turning 60, I participated in events testing balance, agility and more. My score promised to tell me how well I’m aging. The day before my 60th birthday, I arrived at the inaugural Super Age Games in New York City. Perhaps, I thought to myself, I’ll find out I’m only turning 40. The event floor thrummed with pop and hip-hop, while two M.C.s provided running commentary. About 500 other amateur athletes, ranging in age from their 20s to their 80s, milled around the arena. Soon, I would tackle eight “trials,” measuring not only my physical traits such as agility, aerobic fitness and balance, but also my cognitive processing speed and social connection. It felt like it was part track meet, part Senior Olympics, part longevity-enthusiast meet-up. I’d be scored in each category, relative to my gender and age. I would also receive my “Super Age,” based mainly on my aerobic fitness. The organizers claim that, taken together, my scores could help me see how I was performing along key longevity metrics, and could help me forecast my health span and life span. They aren’t whirlpools bursting with light, but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” said Michael Keim, an astrophysicist at Yale University. And this isn’t even the weirdest thing about them. Your weekly roundup of the best stories on health care, the climate crisis, new scientific discoveries, and more. Dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together. It draws ordinary, visible matter toward it, allowing stars to form and keeping the stelliferous limbs of galaxies from flying off. “Almost all galaxies are dominated by dark matter,” said Shyam Balaji, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London. But these three diffuse galaxies, known as DF2, DF4, and DF9, have left astronomers stunned. After using a suite of telescopes to estimate their masses—using the motions of their stars as a proxy—the researchers found that all three have little dark matter. Instead, a pittance of ordinary matter alone must have forged their small selection of stars. How could these rule-breaking galaxies have formed? A paper published in June 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal offers a potential solution. Once upon a time, two regular galaxies collided. Their ordinary matter—their gas and dust—swirled about and got clumped up. But the dark matter passed right through and continued on, like a specter passing through a wall. e5a78b9ce16dabefe27beeb89dbea0ca.text: For decades, doctors have relied on body mass index, or BMI, to diagnose obesity. The calculation—simply a person’s weight divided by their squared height—gained popularity because it was quick and easy to use in a doctor's office. But BMI is far from perfect. It reveals little about an individual’s body composition—is the weight fat or muscle, for example?—and perhaps most importantly, it says little about whether excess body fat is actually affecting a person’s health. Despite these shortcomings, scientists have struggled to come up with a different way to diagnose obesity. But a landmark study published in _Nature_ this week tests an alternative vision that would distinguish between what researchers call clinical obesity—when excess body fat impairs organ function or everyday activities—and preclinical obesity, in which excess body fat is present but function remains intact. The idea was first proposed in January 202500316-4/fulltext) by an international research group writing in the _Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology_. The new study is the first major test of whether it could supplant BMI—and the results are encouraging. The 2025 _Lancet_ study recommended supplementing BMI with measurements such as waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio to better identify excess body fat. It also proposed assessing whether that fat was causing measurable organ dysfunction. In the new study, by analyzing health data from more than 844,000 adults across four countries, the researchers found that BMI both overestimated and underestimated obesity in certain groups compared with the new framework. They also found that people with clinical and preclinical obesity faced markedly different long-term health risks. Most people with preclinical obesity did not go on to develop clinical obesity over a decade, while those with clinical obesity faced a substantially higher risk of death. 84b3b2485345060bba783302f126c7c4.text: Sometimes new species evade detection because they’re tiny and thus easy to miss—not this giant fungus. Shaped like a hand reaching out of the ground, this new species of fungus was discovered deep in the forest in China’s Yunnan Province. A research team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, reported it as a new species they named _Dianjunus rex_. The name comes from the region’s ancient Dian Kingdom and the Chinese pronunciation of the word “fungus.” _D. rex_ is a type of Ascomycete, which is the largest phylum of fungi with over 64,000 known species, and among them, this new fungus produces the largest masses of mushroom recorded. Unlike what we typically think of as a “mushroom,” Ascomycetes don’t form caps and stems but produce structures called fruiting bodies, which release spores to reproduce. It has been edited for length and clarity._ I asked to transfer from Houston to Dallas in my HR role at a leading insurance company because I was very worried about my mom, who lived there. It was June 2024, but she'd been having issues with high anxiety and forgetfulness for around two years. She'd always been very neat. Then she was the opposite. Stacks of papers started to pile up in her house, and she felt overwhelmed by letters from Medicare and about retirement stuff. She loved decorating for each new season, but her fall decor stayed up for a year. She was referred to a neuropsychologist and failed all the tests. Then, after an MRI and a PET scan, she was diagnosed in October 2024 with Alzheimer's disease and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). Stephens noticed that her mom's previously neat house had become cluttered. I wasn't completely surprised. It was the confirmation that made me cry in the clinic. I was glad I'd made the move to Dallas, especially because I was pregnant. At first, Mom stayed in her own house, around 25 minutes away from mine. I had my son in January 2025, and later put him in $1,100-a-month day care while I worked at my office in downtown Dallas. I worked out a routine where my friend would go over and check in on her in the morning. I'd stop by in the evening after picking up the baby. I made sure she ate dinner. af625e32bc4519d1f3670c6852e2fda1.text: VCG/VCG via Getty ImagesFormer OpenAI researcher Paul Christiano warns that rogue AI agents could ultimately escape human control and cause catastrophic accidents. Death by AI may sound like science fiction, but Paul Christiano says it could become the most likely fate for people alive today. "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident," the former OpenAI researcher said at The Hinton Lectures on Monday. Christiano, who leads the Alignment Research Center, warned that increasingly capable AI agents could learn to deceive their human overseers, compromise the systems used to assess them, and ultimately make themselves too powerful to control. He cited OpenAI's agents hacking the open-source repository Hugging Face earlier this year, and a UK AI Security Institute evaluation in which a Claude agent tried to plant malicious code in an open-source package. "I think there is a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years," Christiano said. Christiano was a member of OpenAI's technical staff from 2017 to 2021, according to his LinkedIn. He is now the executive director of the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit that describes itself as focusing on aligning machine learning systems with human interests. His warning adds to a growing debate among researchers over whether increasingly autonomous AI systems could eventually escape meaningful human control and wipe out humanity. The debate intensified in September after Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's alignment stress-testing team, said he believed there was a greater-than-10% chance that AI could kill all humans within a decade. Geoffrey Hinton, the computer scientist widely known as the "Godfather of AI," said a 10% chance of AI-driven human extinction within that period was "not an unreasonable estimate."
